title: Sandboxed Node execution for PTC
summary: Each model-written program for programmatic tool calling runs in a fresh Node process, confined by the same sandbox provider as shell commands and owned by the subprocess service; no worker thread or persistent kernel remains.
firstReason: Per-call process isolation under the session's sandbox policy is kept. Open point for the area owner: a Go host has no Node executable of its own, so the guest runtime must be chosen and located.

title: Reuse the PTC Node sandbox for workflows
summary: Dynamic workflows run model-written JavaScript inside the same sandboxed process runtime as programmatic tool calling instead of a second launcher; the script VM is not treated as a security boundary.
firstReason: One sandboxed guest runtime for all model-written code avoids duplicating confinement and cleanup; keep it, subject to the same guest-runtime question as programmatic tool calling.

title: Node PTC execution modes and in-memory state
summary: The runtime for PTC programs (PTC is the mode in which the model writes a program that calls tools) has two modes: 'per-call' starts a fresh process each time; 'persistent-in-memory' keeps one process per owning agent so variables survive between calls. State kept across restarts ('durable') is explicitly not offered.
firstReason: Interactive automation needs object references to survive between model calls, and tying the state to an explicit owner gives it a clear release point. The runtime is already a child process, so the Go host can supervise it the same way; which JavaScript engine runs the programs is for the PTC area to decide.

title: Retained PTC processes follow file policy
summary: A retained PTC process starts through the same sandbox provider as a per-call one and keeps one resolved file policy until it is released. An approved one-time escalation runs in a fresh temporary environment that cannot see or change the retained variables.
firstReason: A process that outlives one call can also outlive a one-time approval or a policy change, which would be a sandbox escape by retention. The rule is a security invariant for any long-lived child process.

title: PTC Script evaluation and state retention
summary: The PTC runtime treats program syntax and state retention as two separate settings: `programFormat` says what syntax is accepted, `retainsState` says whether variables survive between calls. A 'script' evaluator is added that can run either fresh or retained.
firstReason: Inferring memory lifetime from syntax prevented valid combinations. Two independent settings are the right interface for any runtime. The evaluator internals (Node `vm`, the REPL await transform, the Acorn parser) belong to the JavaScript runtime process and are not host design.

title: Retained PTC interruption
summary: On timeout or cancel of a retained PTC program the host revokes its authority at once and asks the runtime to stop cooperatively. Only if no acknowledgement arrives within a grace period is the process killed, and the result says whether the variables survived.
firstReason: Killing the process on every timeout lost unrelated retained objects. Revoke first, then cooperative stop, then bounded kill is the cancellation pattern for any supervised child process in Go.

title: Scoped REPL evaluator for retained PTC
summary: Retained `run_code` state moves from Node's global REPL scope to a scoped evaluator (a scope-chain kernel plus an evaluator), so a later program may declare a `const`, `let` or `class` name again instead of failing before any statement runs.
firstReason: Models redeclare names across calls whatever the host is written in, so the behaviour must hold. The evaluator is JavaScript that runs inside the program runtime process, not in the host, so it can be carried inside that runtime helper for as long as programs stay TypeScript.
